title: Grace That Trains a Household
summary: Titus must teach every group a life fitting sound doctrine, grounded in saving grace and the hope of Christ’s glorious appearing.
historicalContext: Titus had been left in Crete to bring order to young congregations scattered through its cities. The island had a reputation for dishonesty and excess, and the false teachers described in chapter 1 were unsettling whole households for profit. Most believers lived within the extended Greco-Roman household, where grandparents, married couples, unmarried young men, and slaves shared one roof and one economy. Outsiders judged a new religion largely by what it did to such homes: did it make wives contemptuous, slaves insolent, and young men reckless, or did it make them better? Many converts had spent most of their lives under pagan habits, including heavy drinking and loose speech. Paul therefore asks Titus to show, group by group, how the gospel reshapes ordinary relationships, so that the teaching about God our Saviour would be honoured rather than slandered by those watching from outside.
literaryContext: Chapter 2 opens with an emphatic “But speak thou,” setting Titus against the empty talkers of 1:10–16. Verses 1–10 address older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves, and three purpose clauses show the outward concern: that God’s word not be blasphemed (v. 5), that opponents have nothing evil to say (v. 8), and that slaves adorn the doctrine (v. 10). The connecting “For” of verse 11 then grounds all this conduct in one of Paul’s fullest summaries of salvation. Grace has appeared, grace trains, believers wait for the appearing of glory, and Christ gave Himself to redeem and purify a people. The charge to “speak” in verse 15 closes the unit by echoing verse 1, framing the whole chapter, and chapter 3 extends the same pattern from the household to civic life.
themes: Self-mastery in every season of life
Teaching by example as well as word
Ordinary faithfulness that commends the gospel
The blessed hope of Christ’s glorious appearing

outline.title: Older Believers and Younger Women
outline.summary: Titus teaches what befits sound doctrine, and seasoned men and women model and pass on a disciplined, loving, and pure way of life.

outline.title: Young Men and the Pastor’s Pattern
outline.summary: Younger men are urged toward self-control, and Titus must embody good works and sound teaching that leave opponents with nothing to say.

outline.title: Servants Who Adorn the Doctrine
outline.summary: Slaves who believe are to show honesty and fidelity, so that their lives make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.

outline.title: The Grace That Teaches and the Hope That Waits
outline.summary: God’s saving grace has appeared, trains believers to renounce ungodliness, and directs them to the glorious appearing of Christ, who gave Himself to redeem a people.

outline.title: Teaching with Full Authority
outline.summary: Titus must speak, exhort, and rebuke with God-given authority and let no one disregard him.

verses.bibleText: But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The opening words turn sharply away from the false teachers of chapter 1. They profess to know God while denying Him by their works (1:16); Titus is to be different, and the Greek places the pronoun “thou” in a position of emphasis. Error is not answered merely by denunciation. Paul’s remedy is steady, positive instruction in the truth, set against the noise of the “vain talkers.”

“Speak” here means to teach, and the content of that teaching is defined as “the things which become sound doctrine.” The verb translated “become” describes what is fitting or suitable, what matches its source. Sound doctrine has a corresponding way of life, as a healthy body has a corresponding vigour. The word “sound” carries the language of health that runs through the Pastoral Letters: true teaching makes people whole, while false teaching spreads like disease (2 Timothy 2:17).

The verse therefore introduces everything that follows in verses 2–10. Paul will speak about temperance, love, purity, kindness, honesty, and work, and he regards all of it as an outworking of doctrine. Belief and behaviour cannot be separated without damage to both. A congregation that confesses the truth while living carelessly misrepresents the truth it confesses.

This also guards against a narrow view of ministry. Titus’s pulpit includes kitchens, workshops, and the interactions of old and young. The gospel that saves is the same gospel that shapes how believers speak, eat, drink, labour, and love.

wordNotes.term: ἃ πρέπει τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ (ha prepei tē hygiainousē didaskalia) — the things which become sound doctrine
wordNotes.explanation: Prepei means “is fitting” or “is suitable.” The verb implies a standard: certain conduct belongs with true teaching and other conduct clashes with it. Hygiainousē, “being healthy,” presents doctrine as wholesome and life-giving, in contrast with the unhealthy speculations of the false teachers. The phrase joins what the church believes to the kind of people it produces.

verses.bibleText: That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul begins with the “aged men,” the senior members of the congregation whose example would shape the rest. The word refers to age, not to the office of elder, though the qualities required overlap with those listed for overseers in 1:6–9. Years alone do not produce maturity, and the instruction implies that older believers must keep growing.

Four qualities come first. “Sober” describes freedom from the clouding influence of wine and, by extension, a clear and watchful mind; Scripture consistently warns that strong drink deceives (Proverbs 20:1), and leaders in God’s house are to be free of its grip. “Grave” denotes a dignity that earns respect, a seriousness of purpose that is far from gloom. “Temperate” translates sōphrōn, the sound-minded self-control that recurs throughout this chapter for every group (vv. 2, 4, 5, 6, 12).

The older men must also be “sound in faith, in charity, in patience.” The same word used for sound doctrine in verse 1 is now applied to their inner life. Faith, love, and patient endurance form a familiar Christian triad, with endurance standing where hope often stands (1 Thessalonians 1:3). The substitution suits later life. Age brings particular temptations: faith may stiffen into habit or tradition, love may cool into mere sentiment, and patience may decay into weary resignation. Paul calls for these graces to remain healthy.

An aged believer who trusts God steadily, loves generously, and endures without complaint becomes a living sermon to younger men and women. The congregation needs such fathers in the faith.

wordNotes.term: νηφαλίους (nēphalious) — sober
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective originally described abstaining from wine and came to describe a clear-headed, alert state of mind. Both senses fit Paul’s concern. Freedom from intoxication protects the clarity that spiritual watchfulness requires, and the same term appears among the qualifications for church leaders.

wordNotes.term: ὑπομονῇ (hypomonē) — patience
wordNotes.explanation: This is endurance under pressure, the capacity to remain faithful when trials are long. For older men it guards against bitterness and spiritual fatigue. Its place beside faith and love shows that perseverance is a fruit of grace, not mere temperament.

verses.bibleText: The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Likewise” links the older women to the older men: they share the same calling to maturity, expressed in ways suited to their place in the household. The gospel had raised the dignity of women in a society that often disregarded them, and that new standing invited a corresponding seriousness of life.

Their behaviour is to be “as becometh holiness.” The rare Greek expression was used of what befits a sacred person or a temple servant. Paul pictures older women carrying the reverence of worship into every room of the house. Their demeanour, the visible bearing that reflects inner character, should show that they belong to God.

Two warnings follow. They must not be “false accusers,” a word that literally means slanderers and is used elsewhere of the devil himself. Concern for others can sour into gossip, and the older woman with knowledge of many households is especially exposed to that danger. They must also not be “given to much wine.” The verb means enslaved, a stronger term than the parallel in 1 Timothy 3:8. Many Cretan converts had lived for decades in a culture of heavy drinking, and Paul knows that a habit of years can become bondage. Christ offers freedom from such slavery, and the church’s older women are to show it.

Positively, they are to be “teachers of good things.” The verse that follows defines the setting: they instruct younger women, largely in the home and through friendship. Their teaching is both spoken and lived, and it stands against the old wives’ fables that the false teachers circulated (1 Timothy 4:7). Experience surrendered to Christ becomes a treasure for the next generation.

wordNotes.term: ἱεροπρεπεῖς (hieroprepeis) — as becometh holiness
wordNotes.explanation: The word, found only here in the New Testament, means “befitting what is sacred.” It was used of conduct appropriate to a priest or temple. Applied to older women, it suggests that the whole of life is to bear the dignity of service offered to God.

wordNotes.term: οἴνῳ πολλῷ δεδουλωμένας (oinō pollō dedoulōmenas) — given to much wine
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect participle means “having been enslaved.” Paul describes drinking that has mastered the drinker. The language anticipates the gospel’s promise of freedom from every kind of bondage and fits the Bible’s broader counsel to avoid what clouds judgment and harms the body.

verses.bibleText: That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The older women teach “that they may teach the young women.” Paul does not ask Titus, a young man, to counsel young wives directly; that ministry belongs most fittingly to mature women who have walked the same road. The arrangement protects Titus and the young women alike and honours the experience of older believers.

The verb rendered “teach” here is related to sōphrōn. It means to train someone in sound judgment, to bring a person to a sensible and self-governed way of life. What follows is less a lecture than an apprenticeship.

The first lessons are love: to love their husbands and to love their children. It may seem strange that love needs teaching, yet the New Testament constantly commands love because it does not grow automatically. Marriages can grow cold, and children can be resented as obstacles or left to grow up untended. Love that is patient, faithful, and self-giving is learned through example and practice. The two Greek words, used together in ancient inscriptions honouring good wives, describe affection that acts.

The false teachers were overturning whole households (1:11) and elsewhere disparaged marriage (1 Timothy 4:3). In that setting a home where a wife and mother loves her family with warmth and steadiness becomes a living refutation of error. Paul places such love first because every other virtue in the list grows best in its soil.

wordNotes.term: σωφρονίζωσιν (sōphronizōsin) — teach
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to make someone sound-minded, to train in prudence and self-control. It suggests encouragement and practical guidance. The older women help younger women develop settled judgment for the responsibilities of marriage and motherhood.

wordNotes.term: φιλάνδρους, φιλοτέκνους (philandrous, philoteknous) — to love their husbands, to love their children
wordNotes.explanation: Both compounds appear only here in the New Testament. They describe warm, practical affection within the family. Ancient epitaphs used the pair to praise devoted wives, and Paul adopts it as a Christian ideal that complements the husband’s call to love his wife as Christ loved the church.

verses.bibleText: To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The list continues with five further qualities. “Discreet” translates sōphrōn once again, the self-mastery that subordinates personal impulse to the good of others and meets disappointment with courage. “Chaste” means morally pure in thought and conduct, especially in faithfulness within marriage.

“Keepers at home” follows the reading of many later manuscripts. The better-attested Greek reading means “workers at home,” describing a woman busy and diligent in the management of her household. Proverbs 31 shows how wide that sphere could be: the capable wife buys fields, trades goods, and cares for the poor, all while her household thrives. Paul’s point is not confinement but diligence, and the contrast is with idleness that wanders from house to house (1 Timothy 5:13). The responsibility of nurturing children and ordering a home is a sacred trust that no amount of public activity can replace.

“Good” is best understood as kind, a disposition of goodwill toward family, servants, and neighbours. “Obedient to their own husbands” uses the verb of voluntary submission, not the word used for children or slaves. The submission is to “their own” husbands, not to men in general, and Paul elsewhere sets it within mutual submission and the husband’s Christlike, self-sacrificing love (Ephesians 5:21, 25). It never requires a wife to join in sin, for God must be obeyed first (Acts 5:29), and it does not lessen her equal standing as a fellow heir of grace (1 Peter 3:7).

The purpose clause governs the whole list: “that the word of God be not blasphemed.” Outsiders judged the gospel by the homes it produced. If Christian women became careless, unloving, or contemptuous in the name of their new faith, pagans would conclude that the message made people worse. Paul echoes Isaiah 52:5, where God’s name was reviled because of His people’s conduct. Faithfulness in ordinary household duties becomes a form of witness.

Such counsel was never meant to diminish women. It honours the home as a primary place where the gospel is displayed, and it calls women, as it calls men in the next verses, to a self-controlled and loving life that commends Christ.

wordNotes.term: οἰκουργούς (oikourgous) — keepers at home
wordNotes.explanation: The stronger manuscript reading oikourgous means “working at home,” while the variant oikourous means “staying at home.” The adopted reading emphasises industry rather than seclusion. Paul commends diligent care of the household, a task Scripture treats as honourable and demanding.

wordNotes.term: ὑποτασσομένας τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν (hypotassomenas tois idiois andrasin) — obedient to their own husbands
wordNotes.explanation: The present middle participle describes ongoing, willing self-arrangement under the husband’s leadership. “Their own” limits it to the marriage relationship. In Paul’s letters it stands beside the husband’s call to sacrificial love and the believer’s prior allegiance to God.

verses.bibleText: Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word to young men is the briefest in the chapter, yet it gathers everything into one requirement: they are to be “sober minded.” The verb is the same sōphrōn family already applied to older men and to women (vv. 2, 4, 5). Self-mastery is the common thread binding every age and station together.

Young men face particular pressures: physical strength and ambition, impatience with restraint, the pull of reckless company, and the appetite for recognition. Sound-mindedness answers all of these by bringing desire, temper, and speech under the rule of Christ. Christian self-control differs from the pride of the moral philosopher because it begins with humility and depends on the Spirit, whose fruit it is (Galatians 5:23).

Titus himself is to “exhort” them, a verb that combines urging, encouraging, and appealing. Being young himself (compare 1 Timothy 4:12), he could speak to them as one who shared their struggles. The next verse shows that his own life would be the strongest form of this exhortation.

wordNotes.term: σωφρονεῖν (sōphronein) — to be sober minded
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive means to think and act with sound judgment and restraint. It is not a narrow rule about one vice but a governing disposition that orders the whole life. Its repetition across the chapter shows that self-control is basic to Christian character at every age.

verses.bibleText: In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Titus cannot ask of others what he does not show himself. “In all things” may belong with the previous verse, extending the young men’s self-control to every area, or with this one, describing the range of Titus’s example. Either way the demand is comprehensive.

He is to be “a pattern of good works.” The word typos referred originally to the mark left by a blow or the impression made by a die, and so came to mean a model to be copied. Titus’s life is to leave an imprint on the congregation, especially on the young men he exhorts. Example comes before precept in the sentence, and the order matters. Instruction carries little weight when the teacher’s life contradicts it; consistent conduct gives words their credibility.

Paul then turns to Titus’s teaching. “In doctrine” he must show “uncorruptness,” a soundness untouched by the distortions spreading through Crete. The teaching must be pure in content and pure in motive, free of the greed that drove the false teachers (1:11). “Gravity” describes a dignified seriousness of manner. The teacher of God’s word should not trivialise holy things or court applause with novelty. “Sincerity” is lacking in many early manuscripts and may have entered the text as an explanatory addition, though the idea of integrity is already contained in the other terms.

The whole verse describes ministry as embodied truth. Titus represents Christ and His message to the church and to the watching island. Every pastor, teacher, and parent stands in a similar place, and the call is the same: to live what one teaches and to teach what is true.

wordNotes.term: τύπον καλῶν ἔργων (typon kalōn ergōn) — a pattern of good works
wordNotes.explanation: Typos means an impression, a model, or an example to follow. Paul uses it of himself and of churches whose faith was worth imitating. Kalōn ergōn describes deeds that are good and attractive, a phrase that becomes central to the letter’s message.

wordNotes.term: ἀφθορίαν, σεμνότητα (aphthorian, semnotēta) — uncorruptness, gravity
wordNotes.explanation: Aphthoria, unique in biblical Greek, means freedom from taint or decay, describing teaching that is sound and untouched by error. Semnotēs is a seriousness that commands respect. Together they describe the content and the manner of faithful instruction.

verses.bibleText: Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Titus’s words must be “sound speech, that cannot be condemned.” Sound again means healthy, in harmony with the apostolic message that heals. “That cannot be condemned” does not promise that no one will ever criticise him. It means that there will be no just ground for condemnation. Critics may speak, but the charges will not stick.

“He that is of the contrary part” refers to anyone who opposes the faith, whether the deceivers within the congregations (1:10) or pagans and others outside. Such opponents watch the Christian leader closely, hoping to find a flaw that discredits the message. When his speech and conduct are sound, they are left “ashamed,” exposed by the contrast between their accusations and the facts.

Paul’s phrasing shifts significantly at the end: having no evil thing to say “of you,” or as the best manuscripts read, “of us.” The failure of a leader would be laid at the door of the whole church. Each believer’s conduct reflects on the entire body of Christ, and every Christian carries the reputation of the gospel.

This is the second of three purpose clauses in the chapter that look toward outsiders (vv. 5, 8, 10). Christians cannot control what others say, but they can remove every legitimate occasion for reproach. A life of truthful, gracious speech is one of the most persuasive defences of the faith.

wordNotes.term: λόγον ὑγιῆ ἀκατάγνωστον (logon hygiē akatagnōston) — sound speech, that cannot be condemned
wordNotes.explanation: Logos may refer to Titus’s preaching or his everyday conversation, and both are probably in view. Akatagnōstos, found only here in the New Testament, means not open to rightful censure. Speech that is healthy in content and blameless in character leaves critics without a valid case.

wordNotes.term: φαῦλον (phaulon) — evil thing
wordNotes.explanation: Phaulos means worthless or bad in a moral sense. Paul elsewhere sets it opposite to good in God’s judgment. The concern is not mere social embarrassment but real moral wrongdoing that would discredit the gospel.

verses.bibleText: Exhort servants to be obedient unto their own masters, and to please them well in all things; not answering again;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Slaves form a distinct group in the Cretan congregations, and Paul addresses them directly. That alone was striking. Ancient household instruction normally spoke only to the master about managing his property; here slaves are addressed as moral agents, members of the church, and bearers of the gospel’s honour.

The setting must be understood. Slavery in the Roman world was pervasive, and in many cities perhaps a third of the population was enslaved. It was not based on race. People became slaves through capture in war, kidnapping and piracy, debt, abandonment as infants, or birth to a slave mother. Conditions ranged from the deadly labour of mines to positions of trust as household managers, tutors, physicians, and business agents. Yet in every case one human being was the legal property of another, with little protection against cruelty or sexual exploitation. A Christian slave could not simply leave, and the tiny church had no power to change imperial law.

Within that unjust structure Paul asks believing slaves to “be obedient unto their own masters,” using the same verb of submission found in verse 5 and 3:1. He adds that they should “please them well in all things” and not be “answering again.” Popular literature caricatured slaves as insolent and sly. Christian slaves were to overturn the stereotype by serving with goodwill. Their obedience was never unlimited; no master could command a believer to sin, and their service was ultimately rendered to Christ (Colossians 3:23–24).

The gospel did not endorse the system it addressed. Paul names “menstealers” among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), the very trade that supplied the slave markets. He urges slaves to gain freedom when possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), declares that in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Galatians 3:28), commands masters to give what is just and equal (Colossians 4:1), and asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved” (Philemon 1:16). A master who sits at the Lord’s table beside his slave as an equal heir of grace cannot long treat him as property. Scripture’s trajectory undermines slavery at its root, and Christians were right, in later centuries, to work for its abolition.

wordNotes.term: δούλους (doulous) — servants
wordNotes.explanation: Doulos means a slave, a person legally owned by another, not a hired employee. The KJV’s “servants” can soften this reality. The same word describes believers as slaves of Christ, a reminder that every Christian, slave or free, belongs to one Lord who redeems rather than exploits.

wordNotes.term: μὴ ἀντιλέγοντας (mē antilegontas) — not answering again
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to speak against or contradict. Here it describes insolent talking back and an obstructive spirit. The same word describes the “gainsayers” in 1:9, so Christian slaves are called to the opposite of the false teachers’ contentious attitude.

verses.bibleText: Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two further instructions complete the counsel to slaves, one negative and one positive. “Not purloining” translates a verb meaning to set aside something for oneself, a term for petty theft or embezzlement. Slaves often handled their masters’ goods, money, and business affairs, and small thefts could be hidden easily or excused as wages unjustly withheld. Christian slaves were to refuse such dishonesty, even within a system that wronged them.

Instead they were to show “all good fidelity,” a complete trustworthiness that would be proved over time. The phrase describes reliability in every area of responsibility, the kind of faithfulness Jesus praised in the servant who was faithful over a few things (Matthew 25:21).

The purpose clause lifts this counsel to a remarkable height: “that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.” The verb kosmeō described arranging jewels or ornaments to display their beauty. Paul gives the lowest-ranked members of ancient society a calling of great dignity. Those whom the world regarded as property could make the teaching about God the Saviour shine. The gospel is not improved by human effort, but its beauty becomes visible when it transforms people.

The phrase “God our Saviour” also prepares for verses 11–14. The doctrine slaves are to adorn is the message that God saves, and that He has acted in Christ to redeem people from all iniquity. A slave who lives faithfully demonstrates that this salvation is real. The principle extends to every believer, and those who work today under far freer conditions are equally called to honesty and reliability that commend Christ. At the same time, the dignity Paul gives slaves here is one more sign that the gospel regarded them as persons of worth before God, never as mere property.

wordNotes.term: μὴ νοσφιζομένους (mē nosphizomenous) — not purloining
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to put aside for oneself, to pilfer or embezzle. It appears also of Ananias, who kept back part of the price of his land. Christian honesty extends to small, hidden matters.

wordNotes.term: κοσμῶσιν (kosmōsin) — adorn
wordNotes.explanation: Kosmeō means to arrange, decorate, or adorn, and was used of jewels, garments, and buildings. Faithful conduct sets off the beauty of the gospel as a setting displays a gem. The same verb describes women adorned with good works.

verses.bibleText: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The small word “For” carries great weight. Everything Paul has asked of older men, older women, young wives, young men, Titus, and slaves rests on what God has done. The instructions of verses 1–10 are not a code of respectability floating free of the gospel; they are the fitting response to grace. Here, as often in Paul, ethics grows out of theology, though in this chapter the exhortations come first and the foundation is laid beneath them afterward.

“The grace of God” is His free, unearned favour toward sinners, the heart of Paul’s gospel (Ephesians 2:8). This grace “hath appeared.” The verb, from which the word epiphany comes, was used of a sudden dawning of light and of the arrival of a ruler or deity. Paul refers to a historical event: grace became visible in the birth, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. God had always been gracious, as the Psalms testify, but in Christ His saving purpose stepped into human history in person (2 Timothy 1:9–10).

This grace “bringeth salvation to all men.” The Greek is best read as grace bringing salvation to all people, and the phrase stands deliberately after a list that included slaves. No class is excluded: old and young, men and women, free and enslaved. God desires all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and Christ is the light that shines on every person (John 1:9). The offer is universal, though not everyone accepts it. Grace can be refused, and those who persistently reject it forfeit the life it brings; God does not force His love on anyone.

The verse speaks against two errors at once. It rules out the idea that salvation must be earned by moral effort, since it is grace that brings it. It also rules out a narrow gospel reserved for a privileged few. The same grace that saves the respectable householder saves the slave who serves him, and it calls both to the same table.

wordNotes.term: ἐπεφάνη (epephanē) — hath appeared
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to appear, to become visible, or to shine forth, and is used of light breaking upon those in darkness. Its cognate noun describes Christ’s future appearing in verse 13, so the chapter frames the Christian life between two appearings: grace revealed at His first coming and glory revealed at His return.

wordNotes.term: σωτήριος πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις (sōtērios pasin anthrōpois) — that bringeth salvation to all men
wordNotes.explanation: Sōtērios is an adjective meaning saving or bringing salvation, and the dative “to all people” names the scope of that saving intent. The phrase connects with “God our Saviour” in verse 10 and “our Saviour Jesus Christ” in verse 13. The offer reaches every class and nation without distinction.

verses.bibleText: Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Grace does more than pardon; it teaches. The participle “teaching” translates paideuō, a verb used for raising and educating a child, including correction and discipline. Grace appears here almost as a tutor who takes believers in hand and trains them patiently. The same grace that forgives sin also breaks its power and builds new habits. This is the work of sanctification, and it is as much God’s gift as justification itself.

The training has a negative side: “denying ungodliness and worldly lusts.” To deny is to renounce, to say a decisive no. “Ungodliness” is the root, a life that leaves God out; “worldly lusts” are its many branches, desires that aim no higher than what this present order can offer (1 John 2:15–16). Paul does not condemn created things or bodily life, which God made good. He condemns desire that has made the world its god.

The positive side is the main verb: “we should live.” Three adverbs describe that life. “Soberly” returns to the sōphrōn theme of the chapter, a self-controlled and clear-minded life in relation to oneself. “Righteously” describes upright conduct toward others, honest and just in every dealing. “Godly” names reverent devotion toward God. Self, neighbour, and God are all brought into right order.

All of this takes place “in this present world.” Grace prepares believers for the age to come, but it does not lift them out of the present age. It trains them for life in homes, markets, and congregations now, amid a culture hostile to God and in some cases within unjust structures like slavery. Holiness is to be practised, not merely anticipated.

Paul’s wording answers the fear that grace makes people careless. Paul never treats grace as permission to sin (Romans 6:1–2). Grace received is grace that trains, and a person untouched by its discipline has reason to ask whether it has been received at all.

wordNotes.term: παιδεύουσα (paideuousa) — teaching
wordNotes.explanation: Paideuō means to train, instruct, or discipline, especially as a parent or tutor shapes a child. It includes both instruction and correction. Grace is pictured as an educator forming new habits of life, not merely granting an amnesty for past failure.

wordNotes.term: σωφρόνως καὶ δικαίως καὶ εὐσεβῶς (sōphronōs kai dikaiōs kai eusebōs) — soberly, righteously, and godly
wordNotes.explanation: The three adverbs describe self-control, upright dealings with others, and reverent devotion to God. Together they sum up the whole of a sanctified life. The first picks up the key virtue of verses 2–6, and the third echoes the “truth which is after godliness” of 1:1.

verses.bibleText: Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Grace teaches believers to live in the present while “looking for” the future. The verb means to wait with eager expectation, the posture of Simeon waiting for the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25). The Christian life is lived between two appearings, and the second gives direction and urgency to the first.

The object of that waiting is “that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing.” In Greek a single article governs both nouns, joining them as one reality: the hope is the appearing. Hope in the New Testament is not wishful thinking but confident expectation of what God has promised. It is “blessed” because it brings the fullness of blessing. At Christ’s appearing the righteous dead, who now rest in the sleep of death, will be raised, the living saints will be changed, and together they will meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–53). Eternal life, promised before the world began (1:2), will then be given in full.

The word “appearing” (epiphaneia) denotes a visible manifestation, the same family of words used of grace appearing in verse 11. The KJV’s “glorious appearing” may also be read as “the appearing of the glory.” Either way, the return of Christ will be a public, glorious, and personal event. Jesus will come as He went, visibly and in the clouds (Acts 1:11), with power and great glory, so that every eye shall see Him (Revelation 1:7). Scripture offers no hint of a secret or hidden coming; the blessed hope is the open unveiling of the King before the whole world.

The final phrase, “the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ,” may be read as naming the Father and the Son together, as the KJV renders it. The Greek construction, however, with one article joining “God” and “Saviour,” most naturally refers to one person: “our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ.” Several features support this. The appearing in Paul’s letters is always Christ’s, “God and Saviour” was a familiar single title in that period, and verse 14 continues with “who gave himself,” referring only to Christ. The same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:1. No difficulty arises from this reading, for Paul elsewhere ascribes full deity to Christ (Romans 9:5; Colossians 2:9).

The hope is therefore Christ-centred and ethically powerful. Those who expect to see the great God and Saviour face to face purify themselves even as He is pure (1 John 3:3). Waiting does not make believers idle; it makes them watchful, hopeful, and holy.

wordNotes.term: τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης (tēn makarian elpida kai epiphaneian tēs doxēs) — that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing
wordNotes.explanation: The single article tēn governs both elpida and epiphaneian, presenting the hope and the appearing as one event. Epiphaneia means a visible manifestation and, apart from 2 Timothy 1:10, refers in Paul to Christ’s return. The genitive tēs doxēs may be read adjectivally or as “the appearing of the glory,” the splendour that will surround His coming.

wordNotes.term: τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou) — the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ
wordNotes.explanation: One article governs both “great God” and “Saviour,” which in Greek usage normally signals a single person. The phrase is best understood as “our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ,” a strong confession of Christ’s deity. The KJV rendering is grammatically possible, yet in either case the One who appears is Christ.

verses.bibleText: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The relative pronoun “Who” moves from Christ’s future appearing to His past self-giving. “Gave himself for us” echoes Jesus’ own words that the Son of man came to give His life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). His death was not forced upon Him; He laid down His life of His own accord (John 10:18). The preposition “for” means on behalf of, and in a context of ransom it carries the sense of substitution: He gave Himself in our place.

Two purposes follow. First, “that he might redeem us from all iniquity.” The verb lutroō means to set free by paying a price, the language of releasing captives or slaves. Paul has just addressed slaves, and now he reminds the whole church that every believer was once enslaved and has been bought out of bondage. The phrase “from all iniquity” echoes Psalm 130:8, where the Lord promises to redeem Israel from all his iniquities. “Iniquity” translates anomia, lawlessness. Sin is the transgression of God’s law (1 John 3:4), and Christ redeems His people from lawless living so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in them by the Spirit (Romans 8:4). The cross never abolishes God’s moral standard; it frees believers to love and keep it.

Second, He would “purify unto himself a peculiar people.” Purification removes the defilement of sin, as redemption removes its control. Ezekiel 37:23 promised that God would save His people from their transgressions, cleanse them, and make them His people. That promise is fulfilled in Christ. No ceremony can achieve this inner cleansing; it is the work of Christ Himself through His Spirit.

“Peculiar” in older English meant a personal possession, not something odd. The phrase recalls Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 14:2, where Israel was called God’s special treasure. The church of Jesus Christ, gathered from every nation, now carries the same calling and privilege (1 Peter 2:9). They belong to Him because He bought them.

The last words describe this people as “zealous of good works.” Paul knew misdirected zeal from his own past (Galatians 1:14); here zeal is redeemed and directed toward good. The circle of the chapter is complete. The good works of verses 1–10 are not the cause of salvation but its intended fruit. Christ died to produce a people eager to do what pleases God, and as their High Priest He continues to intercede for them until the work is complete.

wordNotes.term: λυτρώσηται ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας (lytrōsētai hēmas apo pasēs anomias) — redeem us from all iniquity
wordNotes.explanation: Lytroō means to release by payment of a ransom. Anomia is lawlessness, conduct contrary to God’s law. The phrase draws on Psalm 130:8 and teaches that Christ’s redemption delivers believers from every kind of rebellion against God’s will, not only from its penalty.

wordNotes.term: λαὸν περιούσιον (laon periousion) — a peculiar people
wordNotes.explanation: Periousios describes something belonging specially to its owner, a treasured possession. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel as God’s own people. Paul applies the covenant language to all who are redeemed by Christ.

verses.bibleText: These things speak, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no man despise thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“These things speak” returns to the verb that opened the chapter (v. 1), framing everything between as a single charge. “These things” include both the practical instructions of verses 2–10 and the great truths of verses 11–14. Titus is to teach the duties and their gospel foundation together.

Three verbs describe his ministry. He is to “speak,” setting forth the truth plainly. He is to “exhort,” urging and encouraging the people to live by what they hear. He is to “rebuke,” correcting those who resist or drift, whether the false teachers of chapter 1 or members grown careless. Different hearers need different approaches: some need instruction, some need encouragement, and some need firm correction.

All of this is done “with all authority.” The word refers to a command, and Paul elsewhere uses it of God’s own commandment (1:3). Titus’s authority does not come from his age, his personality, or even his office. It rests on the divine message he carries and on the integrity of his life. When he teaches what God has revealed, he speaks with God’s authority, yet always with the gentleness and patience that befit a servant of the Lord (2 Timothy 2:24–25).

“Let no man despise thee” warns against being disregarded. Titus cannot control others’ attitudes, but he can give them no reason for contempt by teaching faithfully, living consistently, and refusing to be intimidated. A minister who handles the word with care and lives what he preaches earns a hearing that critics cannot easily dismiss.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς (meta pasēs epitagēs) — with all authority
wordNotes.explanation: Epitagē means a command or an authoritative order. In Paul’s letters it usually refers to God’s commandment. Titus is to speak with the full authority of the message entrusted to him, not with self-assertion.

wordNotes.term: μηδείς σου περιφρονείτω (mēdeis sou periphroneitō) — let no man despise thee
wordNotes.explanation: Periphroneō means to think around or past someone, to disregard or look down on them. Titus must not allow his teaching to be brushed aside. The parallel charge to Timothy links freedom from contempt to an exemplary life.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would an outsider conclude about the gospel by watching how believers in your congregation live at home and at work?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The grace of God that has appeared in Christ trains every believer, in every station of life, to live with self-control, righteousness, and godliness while waiting for His glorious appearing.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul tie ordinary behaviour so closely to “sound doctrine” in verse 1?
How do the older women and Titus himself teach by example, and what does that require of mentors today?
What does it mean that grace “teaches” and not only forgives?
How should the hope of Christ’s appearing shape choices made “in this present world”?
How does the gospel address slaves as moral agents, and how does its larger message undermine slavery itself?
commonMisunderstandings: Paul’s counsel to slaves does not endorse slavery; it guides believers within an unjust system while the gospel proclaims a brotherhood that dissolves it.
Grace teaching holy living does not mean holiness earns salvation; the training flows from salvation already given.
The “blessed hope” is not an unseen withdrawal of the church but the public, glorious appearing of Christ.
Calling wives to love and to honour their husbands does not place women beneath men in worth or require obedience to sin.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the indicative and the imperative together: what God has done in Christ (vv. 11–14) is the ground and power of what believers are to be (vv. 1–10).
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Receive the grace that has appeared in Jesus Christ, let it train you in the details of daily life, and lift your eyes to His appearing.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s grace has appeared in Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to redeem sinners from lawlessness, trains them in holy living, and will return in glory.
flow: Every person stands in need of rescue from ungodliness and lawlessness.
God’s grace has appeared in Christ, offering salvation to all people.
Christ gave Himself to redeem and purify a people for His own possession.
That same grace trains believers to renounce sin and live soberly, righteously, and godly now.
Believers wait for the visible, glorious appearing of their Saviour.
simpleIllustrations: A gifted teacher does more than pardon a pupil’s mistakes; she patiently trains him until the right way becomes his own.
A setting of gold makes a jewel’s beauty easier to see; a faithful life does the same for the gospel.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you receive the grace that has appeared in Christ and let it begin to train your life today?
cautions: Do not present holy living as the price of acceptance with God.
Do not use verses 9–10 to defend any form of human ownership or workplace abuse.
Do not set dates or speculate about timing when presenting the blessed hope.

reflectionQuestions: Does my everyday conduct make the teaching about God my Saviour more attractive or harder to believe?
Whom am I helping to grow in faith by example as well as by words?
Which “worldly lusts” is grace training me to refuse in this season of my life?
How does looking for Christ’s appearing change the way I spend my time and money?
Where do I need to show “all good fidelity” in my work, even when no one is checking?
